activities.caption: bet before you read on — the compounder's surprise
activities.name: apmGeometricPredict

config.q: An account loses 50% one year, gains 60% the next. The arithmetic average of the two returns reads +5%. Where is the account?
config.why: The geometric reality is −20%: compounding punishes volatility, which is why realised growth always sits below the arithmetic average — the wider the swings, the wider the shortfall.

activities.anchor: the single most used comparison metric
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the performance memo
activities.name: apmSharpeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this performance memo is wrong — click it:
lines: The Sharpe ratio is excess return per unit of total risk.
A fund returning 10% with 15% volatility in a 3% rate world scores about 0.47.
Upside volatility is left out of the denominator — only losses count.
That is why practitioners add drawdown and skew measures alongside it.
As a common currency for return per unit of risk, it organises everything that follows.
config.correction: It punishes upside volatility symmetrically with downside — the σ in the denominator is total, not downside-only; the Sortino ratio is the repair that swaps in downside deviation.
config.why: The measure's known weaknesses are symmetry and its collapse when returns are not bell-shaped — which is exactly why the practitioner's toolkit adds drawdown and skew.

activities.caption: pair each hidden-loss measure with its job
activities.name: apmLossMatch

config.prompt: The measures variance hides — pair each with what it captures:

pairs.right: only returns below target enter the denominator
Sharpe's formula with the downside swap made
worst peak-to-trough loss — whether a strategy survives its investors' nerves
the loss threshold not exceeded 95% of the time — blind to the 5% tail it excludes

config.why: Risk is multidimensional, and any single-number summary embeds a claim about which losses matter — portfolio policy written on variance alone fails in the ways (leverage, illiquidity, skew) that produce the famous blow-ups.

activities.caption: call the free lunch — 60/40 with ρ = 0.2
activities.name: apmSixtyFortyEstimate

config.prompt: The worked mix: 60/40 stocks-and-bonds, σ(stocks) = 16%, σ(bonds) = 6%, ρ = 0.2. The weighted-average risk is 12%. What is the true portfolio risk?
config.why: √0.01071 ≈ 10.4% — the correlation engine bought 1.6 points of risk reduction before any skill, and sweeping the weights like this traces the efficient frontier.

activities.name: apmLimitsBuckets

config.why: Professional construction wraps Markowitz in constraints, shrinkage estimation and scenario overlays — the arithmetic survives as the skeleton, not the whole body.

activities.anchor: rebalance only when weights drift past thresholds
activities.caption: drag the divider — drifting vs rebalanced
activities.name: apmRebalCompare

config.prompt: The same design, two maintenance regimes — drag the divider:

before.label: Left alone
before.text: Winners grow past their weights and the risk budget rides with them; with any spread between asset returns that later mean-reverts, the buy-and-hold compounds less than the constant-mix.

after.label: Rebalanced to targets
after.text: The design is restored — and systematically selling relatively expensive assets to buy relatively cheap ones earns a small diversification return in choppy markets, at the cost of taxes, trading and tracking-error regret.

config.why: The professional compromise is bands rather than calendars — and the pension version is the glide path: target-date funds that start equity-heavy and de-risk toward retirement, automation applied to Markowitz.

activities.caption: pin the hedging asset on the schedule
activities.name: apmNegBetaPlace

config.prompt: A market-hedging asset with β below zero: where does its expected return sit, relative to the risk-free rate?
config.why: Below it: a zero-beta asset earns exactly the risk-free rate, and a hedging asset earns less — it pays for the insurance value it provides the market.
